chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a female slave who had been manumitted in part (mudabbarah) and had run away (abqa) from her master for years, then she returned after her master had died, bringing with her many children and possessions. Two witnesses testified that her master had indeed manumitted her in his lifetime before she ran away. He (peace be upon him) said: 'I hold that she and all that is with her belong to the heirs.' I said: 'Should she not be manumitted from one-third of her master's estate?' He said: 'No, because she ran away while disobedient to Allah and to her master, and the act of running away (abqa) nullified the manumission (tadbir).'

key_terms.أَبَقَتْ: Ran away or absconded from the master
key_terms.التَّدْبِيرُ: The manumission process where a slave is freed upon the master's death
key_terms.مُدَبَّرَةٍ: A slave who is manumitted partially (e.g., one-third or one-half) upon the master's death

ai.seo_question: What happens to a mudabbarah slave who runs away before her master dies?
ai.summary: In this ruling from Imam al-Baqir (AS), the concept of 'abqa' (running away) is treated as an act of disobedience that nullifies the 'tadbir' (manumission upon death), thereby keeping the slave woman and her accumulated wealth within the master's estate for the heirs. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential view that the legal status of a mudabbarah is contingent upon her obedience, distinguishing it from unconditional manumission. The hadith underscores the principle that temporary disobedience can revoke a pending legal benefit, a key nuance in Islamic inheritance and slavery law.
